newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE-Orange and Green, the colours of N.Ireland conflict.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Orange and Green, the colours of N.Ireland conflict.

text.p: They spring from the deep roots of Irish conflict and proclaim themselves "true born Britons".
The Protestant slogans "No Surrender" and "Not An Inch" are age-old mottos of a diehard determination to preserve a British foothold carved by colonist ancestors in Roman Catholic Ireland.

For 300 years, in a conflict of "the Orange and the Green", the Protestants of Northern Ireland have celebrated Dutch King William of Orange for vanquishing Catholic King James's forces and their green standards at the battle of the River Boyne on July 12, 1690.
When the Protestant "marching season" dawns, temperatures rise on both sides and the region walks a sectarian tightrope.
Each summer the 200-year-old Protestant Orange Order marching fraternity bring towns and villages to a halt in contentious commemorative parades that climax on July 12.
Catholics dismissively shut their doors or mount their own protests. They say the boisterous marches, and loud-mouthed youths who gather on the fringes, are menacing and bigoted.
To them, "Orangemen" are a symbol of British colonialism and reminders of an era not so long ago when Protestant rulers kept a stranglehold on political and economic power.
But "Orange" marchers regard the parades as a traditional expression of a Protestant culture and British heritage and accuse Catholics of being fired by anti-British feeling.
Tens of thousands assert the right to "walk the Queen's highway" as their forefathers have done for generations.
Ruddy-faced farmers, town-dwelling artisans and sober-suited office managers, the stalwart Protestant Orangemen proudly declare they are as British as Queen Elizabeth.
DRUMS, SASHES AND FLAGS
In Sunday-best clothes and sporting orange sashes, their leaders strut with silver swords and ceremonial pikes as British flags fly at the head of their columns.
Huge silken banners recall William's victory and scenes from the Bible. Bonfires blaze on the eve of "the Twelfth".
Big "lambeg" drums flailed with canes pound out rhythms that Catholics say strike fear in them at the dead of night.
The sound of droning bagpipes, blaring brass and piercing flute bands fill the air. But the Catholics don't cheer.
The Protestants believe that their religion would be oppressed if Northern Ireland were united with the neighbouring Republic of Ireland, which is 95 per cent Catholic.

They say they mark the Battle of the Boyne because it ensured a Protestant monarchy in Britain and guaranteed religious freedom and citizenship for their "planter" ancestors from England and Scotland who colonised the northern region.
But Catholics believe that Orangemen parade "to show who is master". Nationalist opposition has intensified in recent years in some zones which the parades pass through.
They complain that parades are foisted on them and say the marchers should walk in neutral areas or stay in their own strongholds.
Four-months of some 2,500 processions bring tension to a community already swamped in political uncertainty. This summer is more volatile than most.
During last year's marching season, the region was gripped by turmoil that left a bitterness unmatched in recent years.
DRUMCREE THREE?
This year government ministers and police chiefs fear new clashes arising from a parade on July 6 through a Catholic enclave in Portadown, south of Belfast.
For the past two years an Orange march from a tiny Protestant church at Drumcree, on the outskirts of Portadown, has been the focus of civil unrest.
Catholic residents of the Garvaghy road area of the town don't want the march down their street. Last year police banned the parade but then allowed it after Protestants rioted across the province.
The reaction of Catholics, and militant Irish republicans, was to riot in turn. Damage was put at millions of pounds.
Trying to broker a deal, Britain invited the Portadown rivals to Bosnia-style "proximity talks" near Belfast last week in an attempt to avert what is being called "Drumcree Three."
The Protestant and Catholic representatives were under the same roof but in different rooms, with British officials liaising between them.
In an atmosphere laden with mutual suspicion, no compromise emerged, but efforts to find a solution were continuing right up to the last moment.
